nameStory: The red-jointed fiddler crab gets its name from the distinctive reddish coloring at the joints of its legs and claws, which stand out like tiny crimson bracelets against its darker shell. Like all fiddler crabs, males wave their one oversized claw in the air like a fiddle bow, creating a mesmerizing dance across the mudflats during mating season.
description: The red-jointed fiddler crab is a small marsh crab about the size of a quarter, with males sporting one dramatically oversized claw that can be nearly as big as their entire body. These brownish crabs have distinctive reddish-orange coloring at their leg and claw joints, making them look like they're wearing tiny colored bands. They're one of the most common small creatures you'll see scurrying across salt marsh mudflats, living in burrows they dig in the soft sediment. Despite their small size, their sideways scuttling movement and the males' claw-waving displays make them easy to spot.

idTips.label: Red joints
idTips.description: Look for bright reddish-orange coloring at the joints where the legs and claws bend - like tiny orange rubber bands around each joint that really pop against the brownish shell

idTips.label: Male's giant claw
idTips.description: Males have one claw that's comically oversized compared to their body, often held up and waved slowly in the air with a smooth, hypnotic motion

idTips.label: Burrow holes
idTips.description: Round holes about the diameter of a pencil in muddy areas, often with small piles of rolled mud balls nearby that feel smooth and slightly sticky when fresh

idTips.label: Sideways movement
idTips.description: Distinctive quick, jerky sideways scuttling across the mud, freezing motionless when they sense danger, then darting toward their burrows

idTips.label: Shell texture
idTips.description: Smooth, hard shell that feels like a small smooth pebble, typically muddy brown to grayish-brown with a slightly glossy appearance when wet

habitat: Look for red-jointed fiddler crabs in salt marshes and along muddy banks of tidal creeks and rivers, especially where the water is less salty than typical ocean water. They prefer soft, muddy sediments where they can easily dig their burrows, and you'll often find them quite far inland along tidal rivers - sometimes 30+ miles from the ocean. They're commonly seen alongside spartina grasses and other salt-tolerant marsh plants.

seasonality.spring: Crabs begin emerging from winter burrows as temperatures warm, with males starting to wave their claws and establish territories. Look for fresh burrow holes appearing in the mud.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time with males actively waving their large claws and females moving between burrows. The best time to observe their fascinating social behaviors and courtship displays.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues but slows as temperatures drop. Crabs begin preparing deeper winter burrows and spending more time underground.
seasonality.winter: Most crabs retreat deep into their burrows and become inactive. You might see occasional movement on warmer winter days, but burrow holes may appear abandoned.

funFact: Male red-jointed fiddler crabs can actually regrow their giant claw if they lose it, but the new claw grows on the opposite side of their body - so a right-clawed male becomes a left-clawed male, completely changing his 'handedness' for the rest of his life!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the mud fiddler crab, which lives in the same marshes but lacks the distinctive red-orange joint coloring. Remember: 'Red at the joints, red-jointed it is' - if you see those bright reddish bands at the leg joints, you've found a red-jointed fiddler.
contextualKnowledge: These crabs were recently moved from the genus Uca to Minuca in 2016, so you might still see them listed as Uca minax in older field guides and websites. The scientific name change doesn't affect their identification, but it reflects new understanding of fiddler crab relationships.
compareHints: Red-jointed fiddler crabs are distinguished from their close relative the mud fiddler crab primarily by their bright reddish-orange joint coloring, which mud fiddlers completely lack. Red-jointed fiddlers also prefer areas with lower salt content and venture much farther inland along tidal rivers than mud fiddlers typically do. Both species wave their claws and live in similar muddy habitats, but only the red-jointed sports those telltale colorful 'bracelets' at each joint.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Mud fiddler crabs are much smaller and darker than their cousin, the red-jointed fiddler crab, which grows larger and has distinctive reddish joints on its legs.
